rv.q: Cho, a winner of the Susan Smith Blackburn Prize, imbues her meditation on family interactions with gentle humor and quiet simplicity.
Aubergine delivers a moving meditation on love, loss, and the emotional power of food.
The play itself is a somber meditation on death and, as such, as relentlessly depressing as a three-day wake.
Cho's concept is savory enough to sustain the audience for most of the play... But the focus on sense and memory gets repetitious, and much of the play is lumpy.
There’s a languidness to the proceedings that had me slipping down in my chair.
Julia Cho’s Aubergine – a tender play both incisive and contrived – explores the social and emotional uses of food.
Aubergine is all points and no play.
Aubergine is a provocative, emotionally-effective comedy-drama centered around death, family and gastronomy, and totally delectable.
"Cho's beautiful and immensely sensitive new play...There's so much to chew on here that the occasional misstep barely registers.
Aubergine may make you hungry for a post-performance snack, but it's certainly satisfying theatre.
In "Aubergine," an appealing, lyrical family drama by Julia Cho, life boils down to two essentials — food and death.
But all told, Aubergine is rarely over-sweet, and includes much to savor.
Aubergine’s unnecessary lapses into grandiosity ultimately do not mar its achievements.

Cho's notion of centering the play around food as a way of expressing love is potent, though she switches up ingredients in the second act and a monologue that tries to explain a key element of the father's personality threatens to unmoor the drama.
What ultimately makes “Aubergine” feel a bit undercooked is how rarely the characters actually talk to each other.

Aubergine has a fair number of funny, perceptive, and touching aspects, but, ultimately, it feels too polite, too obviously calculated to provide a sense of uplift, too determined to scrub its central situation of anything too ugly or disturbing.

Between the smart acting, thoughtful prose, and underwhelming production, Aubergine is the theatrical equivalent of a functional yet unmemorable meal: It might fill you up, but it is entirely devoid of flavor.
Full of depth, Aubergine is a quiet play in many ways, yet it is incredibly moving.
Julia Cho’s touching play has all the elements of comfort food, it’s a work that knows when to touch what button without being obvious or heavy handed.
At first the show is a sleeper, but it wakes up in the second act to a profound experience.

Cho seems to have been inspired by the death of her own dad and so I feel a bit cold-hearted saying this but Aubergine's Proustian allusions to the memories food evokes, the connections it reinforces didn't seem all that fresh to me.
Red alert! There’s an energy drain at Playwrights Horizons, where Julia Cho’s Aubergine is currently in residence, and no one seems to know how to stop it.
Aubergine is a play that everyone must see!
